articles.title: JupyterHub exposure needs separate user, admin, and service authority
articles.excerpt: JupyterHub exposure needs separate user, admin, and service authority JupyterHub coordinates authentication, user servers, and a proxy. Its value is that a data team can start notebooks without sharin…
articles.body: JupyterHub exposure needs separate user, admin, and service authority JupyterHub coordinates authentication, user servers, and a proxy. Its value is that a data team can start notebooks without sharing one host account. Its risk is similar: the hub can act as an identity broker and a control plane for every user server. A public hub is not necessarily unsafe, but the difference between a user, an administrator, and a service token must be explicit. At about 23:48 UTC on 29 October 2026, count-only ZoomEye SDK queries with sub_type=all and page size 1 returned 0 matches for app="JupyterHub" and 29,791 for title="JupyterHub" . The title query is the only useful observation in this set.

articles.title: Python Steering Council Halts Native JIT Compiler Development Due to Maintenance and Compatibility Concerns
articles.excerpt: Introduction: The Python JIT Dilemma In June, the Python Steering Council made a decision that sent ripples through the developer community: they paused development on the native Just-In-Time (JIT) co…
articles.body: Introduction: The Python JIT Dilemma In June, the Python Steering Council made a decision that sent ripples through the developer community: they paused development on the native Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler for CPython, effectively shelving a project once hailed as a performance game-changer. This move wasn’t arbitrary. It was the culmination of months of debate, technical challenges, and a stark realization: the project’s maintenance burden and compatibility risks outweighed its potential benefits. The JIT compiler, designed to accelerate Python’s execution speed by compiling bytecode to machine code on the fly, promised to bridge the performance gap with languages like Java or C++.
articles.author: Artyom Kornilov

articles.title: The SQL NOT IN Trap: When NULL Quietly Breaks Your Query
articles.excerpt: Some SQL bugs don't throw errors. The query runs, the tests pass, and everything looks fine until a cleanup job skips records it was supposed to catch. One of the reasons this happens is NULL inside a…
articles.body: Some SQL bugs don't throw errors. The query runs, the tests pass, and everything looks fine until a cleanup job skips records it was supposed to catch. One of the reasons this happens is NULL inside a NOT IN query. When NOT IN stops behaving as expected Imagine you're working on a multi-tenant platform. You have a memberships table and an identity_mappings table. Each mapping connects an external identity to a tenant. You need to find memberships that don't have a corresponding identity mapping. A first attempt might look like this: SELECT m . tenant_id , m . external_id FROM memberships m WHERE m . external_id NOT IN ( SELECT i . external_id FROM identity_mappings i ); Nothing looks wrong at first glance. You're selecting external IDs that don't exist in the mapping table.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 29, 1991: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by asteroid Gaspra and snaps amazing photos while flying at 18,000 mph
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Gaspra was the first asteroid to ever be visited by a spacecraft. Gaspra orbits near the inner edge of the asteroid belt . The Galileo spacecraft had been travelling through the asteroid belt for about two months before it reached Gaspra. Galileo was 990 miles (1,593 kilometers) away from Gaspra when it whizzed by, and it was travelling at a relative speed of about 5 miles (8 km) per second. The spacecraft took several photos of the asteroid and used an instrument called the Near-Infrared Mapping Spectrometer to study its chemical composition and other physical properties. Galileo determined that Gaspra has an irregular and elongated shape measuring about 12 miles long and 7 miles wide.

articles.title: Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman named deputy director for NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
articles.excerpt: The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty.
articles.body: The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty. All four astronauts of the Artemis II mission, which flew around the moon in April, have hung up their spacesuits and moved on to greener pastures. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), managed by Caltech, announced yesterday that former NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman will step into the role of Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of JPL, beginning Nov. 30. "Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a JPL press release .

articles.title: Astronauts deploy solar array on 100th US spacewalk by International Space Station crew members
articles.excerpt: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency deployed a new solar array on Thursday (Oct. 29) during a seven-hour spacewalk outside the International Space Station.
articles.body: Two astronauts successfully installed and deployed the second-to-last upgraded solar array for the International Space Station (ISS) during the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the orbiting outpost. Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), both ISS Expedition 75 crewmates, completed the 7-hour-and-11-minute extravehicular activity (EVA) at 3:08 p.m. EDT (1908 GMT) on Thursday (Oct. 29). The spacewalk began and ended inside the U.S. Quest airlock, with both astronauts wearing NASA's extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuits. It was the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019, when David Saint-Jacques ventured into the void with NASA's Anne McClain.
